lessons.name: Determine multiple themes of short stories

content.text: Read the following story.

textContent.text: Simon was accustomed to hearing the crowd screaming when he made a long catch or juked a defender for a touchdown, which is why it was so jarring to hear the stadium suddenly fall silent. He had caught the ball cleanly and seen nothing but open field in front of him. But then a defender appeared out of nowhere, hitting him low and taking him down hard. As he lay on his back in front of the stunned crowd, pain shooting through his knee, Simon could already picture his season slipping away—maybe even his future in football.

An MRI the next morning revealed bad news. "Partial tear of the anterior cruciate ligament," the doctor had said, with an average recovery time of six to nine months. In other words, Simon would be lucky to be back on the field for the start of next season.

For days after his diagnosis, Simon dragged himself through classes at school, barely speaking, and spent his evenings zoning out in front of the TV, ignoring the concerned text messages from teammates.

The night of the next game, Simon's coach set up a folding chair for him on the sidelines. At first, Simon just clapped and called out encouragements, but it felt hollow. Every cheer reminded him that he wasn't out there.
During a timeout, the coach handed Simon one of the tablets they used for game planning. "Make yourself useful," he said with a grin before turning back to the field.

Simon stared after him for a moment, unsure what to do. But as the opposing team broke the huddle and lined up for the next play, something clicked. He'd seen this formation before in the videos his coach put together, but his team's defense wasn't in the right position to stop what was coming.
"Watch the sweep!" he called out, waving a crutch toward the field.

His teammates shifted just before the ball was snapped and tackled the runner behind the line. For the rest of the game, Simon stayed busy—calling out cues, keeping notes, and shouting reminders between downs. When the final whistle blew, his voice was hoarse and his heart was pounding like he'd played every snap himself. For now, he'd lost his spot on the field, but his season was far from over.

choices.text: When setbacks first happen, they often feel like catastrophes.
Disappointment can offer the chance to grow and find new purpose.
During difficult times, it's important to keep your friends close.
Being overly competitive can make it harder to enjoy what you love.

content.text: Read the following story.

textContent.text: Amina stared at the "C+" on her essay, as if the grade itself were a mistake. English had always been easy for her. Her essays usually came back covered in compliments, not red ink.

pieces.text: As the bell rang and students filed into the hallway, Amina remained at her desk, flipping through the margins filled with notes—

content.text: unclear claim, missing evidence, vague

pieces.text: . The feedback stung, and the more she read, the hotter her face felt.

textContent.text: The assignment had been ridiculous, she told herself, and the rumors about Ms. Lin being an unfair grader were true. Everyone always told Amina she was a good writer—she didn't need outlines or color-coded charts or whatever time-wasting "strategies" Ms. Lin had been teaching. Writing came naturally to Amina.
Once her classmates had finally left the room, Amina stood and approached Ms. Lin's desk, clutching the paper so tightly her fingers trembled.
"I don't understand," she said. "I've always been good at writing."

pieces.text: Ms. Lin nodded calmly. "You

content.text: are

pieces.text: good at writing. But this class isn't just about talent. It's about technique—using the tools we've been learning to make your ideas stronger." She smoothed out the crumpled rubric and pointed to the categories Amina had skipped over: structure, evidence, reasoning. "Let's look at where your work shines and where it can grow."

textContent.text: Amina followed along, reluctant at first, but as Ms. Lin explained, she began to see her writing in a new light. The sentences sounded great—that part had been easy—but when she sat with them for a moment, she started to wonder what she had meant by them. At the time, she felt like she had all the right ideas, but they hadn't come together the way she'd remembered.

That night, she rewrote her essay from scratch. The words and sentences still flowed easily, but she took the time to slow down, rethink her ideas, and shape them into something stronger. It took hours, but when she finished, she felt a flicker of pride. The essay read differently now: less effortless, maybe, but far more logical and precise.
When her next paper came back with a bright "B+" at the top, Amina grinned. She'd been hoping for an "A," but hey—it turned out that writing was a process.

textContent.text: Aaron crouched low in the goal, concentrating on every puck that came flying at him. He snatched one with his glove, then dropped to his knees to block another with his pads.
"All right, that's enough! Bring it in!" Coach Quinn's voice boomed, ending the pregame warm-up. Aaron's team gathered around the bench, with Aaron drifting to the back of the semicircle, as usual.
"We're up against a team with size," the coach began. "They'll try to muscle us, so we need to fight fire with fire." He turned to Diego. "You're sitting tonight. I need bigger bodies out there."

Aaron frowned: Diego's speed was exactly what they needed against bigger, slower opponents, but the thought of contradicting Coach Quinn made his throat tighten. Coach had led them through so many tough games—Aaron couldn't imagine telling him he was wrong. He shifted his weight, opened his mouth, then shut it again.

pieces.text: When the game started, Aaron threw himself into blocking shots, but his teammates struggled. Their opponents

content.text: were

pieces.text: big and used their strength to win every battle along the boards. Aaron's gaze kept slipping to the bench where Diego sat, helmet in his lap.

textContent.text: Late in the final period, Coach signaled for a timeout, and the team huddled, sweat steaming off their shoulders. Aaron's chest tightened.
"Um—Coach?" His voice cracked. The circle fell silent, and Aaron's face burned under his mask. He swallowed hard. "Diego could outmaneuver these guys. They're big, but they can't catch him."

For a beat, no one moved. Then, Coach Quinn's brow furrowed and he gave a short nod. "All right. Diego—get out there." When play resumed, Diego darted forward like a blur, slipping between two defenders who had been muscling everyone else out of the way.
Aaron watched Diego cut sharply across the rink and fire a quick pass that set up a shot on goal. Aaron grinned as the puck hit the back of the net and the arena erupted.

textContent.text: "Good morning, everyone! It's Magnificent Monday!" Ms. Tammy called out, waving children and parents across the street as she held her stop sign high in the air. Beside her stood Carla, her soon-to-be replacement, watching the procession closely.
"See that girl there? The one with the sparkly shoes," Ms. Tammy said, nodding toward a young girl tugging at her father's arm. "Ella always tries to run ahead, so keep an eye on her."
Carla nodded.

"And that's Jordan—pretends he's too old for stickers, but his mom told me he keeps every one I give him. And there's Milo—he's always running late but never forgets to stop for a hug." A small boy dashed up and gave Ms. Tammy a quick squeeze. "You really do know everyone," Carla said, impressed. "How do you remember them all?"
Ms. Tammy laughed. "Oh, that's easy—they're my kids."
Carla raised an eyebrow.
"Not my actual kids, of course, but when you treat them like they're your own, it's easy to remember who's got a loose tooth and who's always nervous before a math test."
"Sounds like there's a lot more to this job than just holding a stop sign."

Ms. Tammy shrugged. "Some days it's a lot, sure—your feet ache, the weather doesn't cooperate. But then one of them runs up for a high five, or the quiet kid who never smiles gives you a grin, and suddenly, you forget the difficult parts. This job builds you up more than it wears you down."

As more students approached the crosswalk, Ms. Tammy continued greeting them by name, her warmth rippling through the morning crowd. "You know, I've been out here long enough that some of my kids have grown up. A few even stop by now and then, just to say hello. When you really see people, you don't forget them—and they don't forget you, either."
Carla watched a child hand Ms. Tammy a colorful drawing, and she felt the truth of her words: that a little care had a way of coming back around.

textContent.text: Isabella circled the room, taking in the strange but familiar sights. Here was the corner where she'd sharpened her pencils, the cubby where she'd tucked her lunchbox, the rug where she and her best friend Stella had assembled countless jigsaw puzzles. She smiled as she sat down behind the teacher's desk. The classroom looked the same as it had years ago when she was a young student, but now the space was hers to run as a brand new teacher.

Isabella had pictured a smooth first day, her students hanging on every word, her plans unfolding just as she'd rehearsed. It didn't take long, however, for her confidence to fade. During math, several students argued over supplies, and her carefully planned geography game dissolved into chaos. Reading time went too long, which made her class late for music, and then Isabella spent so much time setting out materials for a science activity that she was late to pick them up.
After dismissal, she began gathering workbooks and reshelving them. Her eyes blurred, and before she knew it, tears were streaking her cheeks.
With a soft knock at the door, Mrs. Highsmith from across the hall peeked in. "Tough day?" she asked gently.
Isabella nodded, wiping at her eyes. "I thought I'd be better at this."
The older woman stepped inside and began picking up scraps of construction paper. "How long have you been teaching, Isabella?"
Isabella gave a shaky laugh. "One whole day."
"Exactly," Mrs. Highsmith replied. "And do you remember how long it took you to learn all the state capitals?"
Isabella smiled at the memory. "I was terrible with capitals. I stayed after school with you every day for weeks, drilling with those flashcards. But in the end, I aced your quiz."

Mrs. Highsmith didn't say anything—just raised her eyebrows knowingly. Isabella sat back, turning the thought over. She had needed a lot of practice before the answers stuck. Teaching was probably the same—maybe she just needed to give herself that same space to grow.
The knot in Isabella's chest loosened. "Thanks, Mrs. Highsmith—I needed that."
"Please—call me Margaret."
Isabella laughed again, shaking her head. She didn't think she would ever be able to do that!

text.text: <atomic>Isabella circled the room, taking in the strange but familiar sights. Here was the corner where she'd sharpened her pencils, the cubby where she'd tucked her lunchbox, the rug where she and her best friend Stella had assembled countless jigsaw puzzles.</atomic>

<atomic>She smiled as she sat down behind the teacher's desk. The classroom looked the same as it had years ago when she was a young student, but now the space was hers to run as a brand new teacher.</atomic>
<atomic>Isabella had pictured a smooth first day, her students hanging on every word, her plans unfolding just as she'd rehearsed. It didn't take long, however, for her confidence to fade.</atomic>

<atomic>During math, several students argued over supplies, and her carefully planned geography game dissolved into chaos. Reading time went too long, which made her class late for music, and then Isabella spent so much time setting out materials for a science activity that she was late to pick them up.</atomic>
<atomic>After dismissal, she began gathering workbooks and reshelving them. Her eyes blurred, and before she knew it, tears were streaking her cheeks.</atomic>
<atomic>With a soft knock at the door, Mrs. Highsmith from across the hall peeked in. "Tough day?" she asked gently.</atomic>
<atomic>Isabella nodded, wiping at her eyes. "I thought I'd be better at this."</atomic>
<atomic>The older woman stepped inside and began picking up scraps of construction paper. "How long have you been teaching, Isabella?"</atomic>
<atomic>Isabella gave a shaky laugh. "One whole day."</atomic>
<atomic>"Exactly," Mrs. Highsmith replied. "And do you remember how long it took you to learn all the state capitals?"</atomic>
<atomic>Isabella smiled at the memory. "I was terrible with capitals. I stayed after school with you every day for weeks, drilling with those flashcards. But in the end, I aced your quiz."</atomic>
<atomic>Mrs. Highsmith didn't say anything—just raised her eyebrows knowingly. Isabella sat back, turning the thought over.</atomic>
<atomic>She had needed a lot of practice before the answers stuck. Teaching was probably the same—maybe she just needed to give herself that same space to grow.</atomic>
<atomic>The knot in Isabella's chest loosened. "Thanks, Mrs. Highsmith—I needed that."</atomic>
<atomic>"Please—call me Margaret."</atomic>
<atomic>Isabella laughed again, shaking her head. She didn't think she would ever be able to do that!</atomic>

textContent.text: Alicia slowed as she passed her teammates, who were laughing together near the front of the plane. She offered a small wave before continuing down the aisle, quietly cursing the computer error that had issued her a seat far from her friends. She hugged her backpack tighter and braced herself for the agony of a five-hour flight with strangers.
When she reached her row, a man in a business suit and an elderly woman carefully stood to let her take her seat by the window.
"Hello, dear," the woman said, settling gingerly back into her seat.

"Hi," Alicia replied, slipping in her earbuds. She could already picture the kind of small talk that would follow—exactly like her grandmother's, friendly but miles away from anything Alicia actually cared about.
"Are you visiting family?" the woman asked.
Alicia considered pretending not to hear, but that felt too rude. With a sigh, she tugged out one earbud.
"Me? No—I'm going to a competition. My team's up there." Alicia pointed to the front of the plane, hoping this would end the conversation.
"Oh? What kind of competition?"
Annoyed, Alicia replied, "I'm a gymnast."
"Gymnastics!" The woman clapped her hands together with delight. "I adore gymnastics!"
Alicia nodded. She got that a lot. People always seemed to love gymnastics even when they knew virtually nothing about it.
"My favorite event was always the balance beam," the woman chuckled. "Beam was the only event that kept me in the running for Montreal in '76."

textContent.text: "Almost," the woman said. "Didn't quite make the cut, but I learned plenty chasing it."

For the rest of the flight, Alicia and the woman traded stories—Alicia describing the challenges of balancing school, travel, and endless training, and the woman sharing how she missed her junior prom to compete at a meet in Budapest. "It was a hard choice at the time," she said, "but the sacrifice was worth it."
Once the plane touched down and she had her bag, Alicia waved goodbye to her seatmate. She couldn't wait to tell the rest of the team about this.

<atomic>After the show, parents and teachers praised the actors, but just as many complimented the beautiful set. Kanchan's heart swelled—her talents had found their place in the spotlight after all.</atomic>

<atomic>Just then, the door at the back of the auditorium swung open, and Mr. Pinkard, the technical director, stepped inside, carrying an enormous sheet of plywood.</atomic>

<atomic>"Sorry for the interruption," he said, winded. "I just wanted to let everyone know I'm still looking for a few students to join the tech crew—set builders, sound and lighting operators, stage managers, that sort of thing."</atomic>
Kanchan straightened a little. I could do that, she thought. Although she wasn't much of a singer, she had an eye for design, and her art teacher frequently singled out her projects as examples.
<atomic>"You've got this," she whispered to her friends, backing out of line and hoping no one else would notice her quiet exit from the lineup.</atomic>
<atomic>Backstage, Mr. Pinkard offered a welcoming smile as she approached. "Looking for something a bit more behind the scenes?"</atomic>
<atomic>Over the next few weeks, Kanchan learned more than she ever expected—how to frame walls, paint scenery flats, and even use power tools.</atomic>
<atomic>During rehearsals, Charlotte and Willow practiced their lines under the bright lights while Kanchan led the crew in moving set pieces between scenes.</atomic>
<atomic>On opening night, the stage glowed beneath painted arches and carefully constructed towers. As the curtain rose, the audience gasped, then burst into applause.</atomic>

<atomic>After the show, parents and teachers praised the actors, but just as many complimented the beautiful set. Kanchan's heart swelled—her talents had found their place in the spotlight after all.</atomic>

textContent.text: Simon was accustomed to hearing the crowd screaming when he made a long catch or juked a defender for a touchdown, which is why it was so jarring to hear the stadium suddenly fall silent. He had caught the ball cleanly and seen nothing but open field in front of him. But then a defender appeared out of nowhere, hitting him low and taking him down hard. As he lay on his back in front of the stunned crowd, pain shooting through his knee, Simon could already picture his season slipping away—maybe even his future in football.

An MRI the next morning revealed bad news. "Partial tear of the anterior cruciate ligament," the doctor had said, with an average recovery time of six to nine months. In other words, Simon would be lucky to be back on the field for the start of next season.

For days after his diagnosis, Simon dragged himself through classes at school, barely speaking, and spent his evenings zoning out in front of the TV, ignoring the concerned text messages from teammates.

The night of the next game, Simon's coach set up a folding chair for him on the sidelines. At first, Simon just clapped and called out encouragements, but it felt hollow. Every cheer reminded him that he wasn't out there.
During a timeout, the coach handed Simon one of the tablets they used for game planning. "Make yourself useful," he said with a grin before turning back to the field.

Simon stared after him for a moment, unsure what to do. But as the opposing team broke the huddle and lined up for the next play, something clicked. He'd seen this formation before in the videos his coach put together, but his team's defense wasn't in the right position to stop what was coming.
"Watch the sweep!" he called out, waving a crutch toward the field.

His teammates shifted just before the ball was snapped and tackled the runner behind the line. For the rest of the game, Simon stayed busy—calling out cues, keeping notes, and shouting reminders between downs. When the final whistle blew, his voice was hoarse and his heart was pounding like he'd played every snap himself. For now, he'd lost his spot on the field, but his season was far from over.

Jason tried to answer, but with his mouth wide open, his reply sounded more like a drawn-out groan. When the hygienist paused to adjust the light, Jason closed his eyes and breathed out slowly, feeling the calm settle in.

content.text: dentist

pieces.text: made his stomach twist. He used to dread the moment his name would be called and he'd be sent back to the exam room. Getting X-rays always freaked him out the most—the heavy apron felt as if it was pinning him down, and the beeps and whirs of the machine sounded like a mechanical monster coming to life behind the wall.

textContent.text: Eventually, though, his mom came up with a way to help him settle down. She taught him to count his breaths—slowly in, slowly out—giving him something else to focus on, something steady that he was in charge of. It worked, and ever since, he had used the same technique not just at the dentist, but anytime he felt nervous or overwhelmed.
"All done!" chirped the hygienist. "You can pick up your school note at reception."

Jason gathered his little plastic bag with the new toothbrush and toothpaste and headed to the waiting room, where he noticed a small girl sitting with her feet under her, clutching a stuffed panda. Her mother whispered something to her, but the girl's eyes stayed wide and anxious.

Jason tried to answer, but with his mouth wide open, his reply sounded more like a drawn-out groan. When the hygienist paused to adjust the light, Jason closed his eyes and breathed out slowly, feeling the calm settle in.

pieces.text: When he was little, just the word

content.text: dentist

pieces.text: made his stomach twist. He used to dread the moment his name would be called and he'd be sent back to the exam room. Getting X-rays always freaked him out the most—the heavy apron felt as if it was pinning him down, and the beeps and whirs of the machine sounded like a mechanical monster coming to life behind the wall.

textContent.text: Eventually, though, his mom came up with a way to help him settle down. She taught him to count his breaths—slowly in, slowly out—giving him something else to focus on, something steady that he was in charge of. It worked, and ever since, he had used the same technique not just at the dentist, but anytime he felt nervous or overwhelmed.
"All done!" chirped the hygienist. "You can pick up your school note at reception."

Jason gathered his little plastic bag with the new toothbrush and toothpaste and headed to the waiting room, where he noticed a small girl sitting with her feet under her, clutching a stuffed panda. Her mother whispered something to her, but the girl's eyes stayed wide and anxious.

pieces.text: Jason hesitated, then crouched beside her. "Hey," he said softly. "I used to be scared here, too. You know what helped me?" The girl stared at him, still hugging her panda. "When the machines start making those weird sounds, I just count my breaths—

content.text: one, two, three

pieces.text: —until it's over. It helps me relax."
For a moment, she studied Jason as if deciding whether to believe him. Then she gave a small nod, closed her eyes, and took some deep breaths, mouthing

content.text: one, two, three

pieces.text: . Jason watched as her shoulders dropped slightly and her fingers loosened around the panda's paw.

content.text: two

pieces.text: themes are found in the story?

pieces.text: A

content.text: theme

pieces.text: is the

content.text: central message or lesson

pieces.text: communicated in a story, poem, or play. Some stories have one main theme, while others explore multiple themes. In most stories, themes are not directly stated. You have to infer them by thinking about the details in the text.

content.text: Finding the Theme

pieces.text: To determine the theme, start by looking at the characters and events in the story. Pay attention to conflicts the characters experience and how they respond to them. Then, think about how the characters and events might connect to

content.text: a larger lesson or truth

pieces.text: . Ask yourself if the story teaches you anything about the world, or provides any lessons that you could apply to your own life.

content.text: Using Text Evidence

pieces.text: Themes are supported by

content.text: text evidence

pieces.text: . To find good evidence, look for actions, events, or dialogue that show what the author is trying to communicate.

contents.text: The purpose of an advertisement is to persuade people to do something. To accomplish this purpose, advertisements use three types of persuasive strategies, or appeals:

header.text: Appeals to ethos, or character, show that the writer or speaker is trustworthy or is an authority on a subject. An ad that appeals to ethos might do one of the following:

elements.text: say that a brand has been trusted for many years
note that a brand is recommended by a respected organization or celebrity
include a quote from a "real person" who shares the audience's values

header.text: Appeals to logos, or reason, use logic and specific evidence. An ad that appeals to logos might do one of the following:

elements.text: use graphs or charts to display information
mention the results of scientific studies
explain the science behind a product or service

header.text: Appeals to pathos, or emotion, use feelings rather than facts to persuade the audience. An ad that appeals to pathos might do one of the following:

elements.text: trigger a fear, such as the fear of embarrassment
appeal to a desire, such as the desire to appear attractive
link the product to a positive feeling, such as adventure, love, or luxury

header.text: Appeals to ethos, or character, show that the writer or speaker is trustworthy or is an authority on a subject. An ad that appeals to ethos might do one of the following:

elements.text: say that a brand has been trusted for many years
note that a brand is recommended by a respected organization or celebrity
include a quote from a "real person" who shares the audience's values

header.text: Appeals to logos, or reason, use logic and specific evidence. An ad that appeals to logos might do one of the following:

elements.text: use graphs or charts to display information
mention the results of scientific studies
explain the science behind a product or service

header.text: Appeals to pathos, or emotion, use feelings rather than facts to persuade the audience. An ad that appeals to pathos might do one of the following:

elements.text: trigger a fear, such as the fear of embarrassment
appeal to a desire, such as the desire to appear attractive
link the product to a positive feeling, such as adventure, love, or luxury

content.text: Bias

pieces.text: results when writers inject personal feelings or opinions into writing that is supposed to be neutral and fact-based.

content.text: Positive bias

pieces.text: occurs when writers use language showing that they like or agree with the subject they are writing about.

content.text: Negative bias

pieces.text: occurs when writers use language showing that they dislike or disagree with the subject.

contents.text: When completing a research assignment, you should try to find sources that are reliable and free from bias. One way to check for bias in a news story is to look at the language used in the story's headline. A headline that includes highly emotional or opinion-based language is a sign the story might be biased.
These headlines use biased language:

lines.text: Well-Designed Construction Plan an Absolute Win for Community

content.text: Language like "well-designed" and "absolute win" suggests the writer has a positive bias toward the construction plan.

lines.text: Flawed Construction Plan Too Risky for Community

content.text: Language like "flawed" and "too risky" suggests the writer has a negative bias against the construction plan.

contents.text: This headline avoids biased language:

lines.text: Study Examines Impacts of Construction Plan on Community

content.text: The language used in the headline does not reveal the writer's own feelings about the construction plan.
